sources.title: Dutch National Archives, States General resolutions
sources.note: Seven-province confederation governed through States General from 1588 to 1795; provinces retained autonomy.

sources.title: Dutch National Archives, Act of Abjuration
sources.note: 1581 break with Philip II preceded the republic established in 1588; declaration was printed and circulated.

sources.title: Dutch National Archives, Peace of Münster 1648
sources.note: Spain recognized the republic as independent in 1648; treaty also dealt with overseas holdings and religious limits.

sources.title: Dutch National Archives, Batavian Revolution 1795
sources.note: French forces and Dutch Patriots ended the old republic; Batavian Republic proclaimed 20 January 1795.

sources.title: Dutch National Archives, VOC 1602–1800
sources.note: 1602 trading company received broad state powers and used violence in Asian trade.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, Colonial Trade
sources.note: VOC and WIC trade depended on coercion, war and slave labor as well as goods and investment.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, West India Company
sources.note: WIC traded gold and enslaved people, transported captives across the Atlantic and fought colonial wars.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, Seventeenth-century galleries
sources.note: Rembrandt, Vermeer, Hals and Steen produced celebrated paintings during the republic’s commercial and scholarly expansion.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, Ten things about home in the seventeenth century
sources.note: Open doors, household work, linen washing, a child’s potty chair, board games and pregnancy customs.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, Women’s work in the seventeenth century
sources.note: Many women earned income as well as managing households, countering the idle-housewife stereotype.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, Petronella Oortman’s dolls’ house
sources.note: Wealthy display object with kitchens, laundry, books, lying-in room and miniature running water; not a typical home.

sources.title: Amsterdam City Archives, Jordaan household archaeology
sources.note: Cesspits from modest seventeenth-century homes preserve dishes and imported porcelain fragments.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, The Schoolmaster
sources.note: Painting shows a schoolmaster with boy and girl pupils, hourglass, papers and writing.

sources.title: Dutch National Archives, Siege of Den Bosch and war news
sources.note: Printed news maps and newspapers spread accounts of military events among republic residents.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, Republic coat of arms on engraved glass
sources.note: An engraved glass dated 1600 bears the original Latin motto Concordia res parvae crescunt.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, At Home in the Seventeenth Century
sources.note: Households ranged from rich to poor, migrants to merchants, Protestant to Jewish and Catholic; material culture varied.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Imported c. 1600 to 1783 interval is map coverage, not the republic’s 1588 to 1795 lifespan. Its polygon remains unverified.

Domestic evidence comes from specific museum objects, paintings and Amsterdam archaeology; it must not stand for all regions or income groups. Colonial violence is attributed to the companies and political structures, not every Dutch person. Narrative awaits independent review.

aliases: Republic of the Seven United Netherlands
proposedOverrides.summary: The Dutch Republic was a confederation of seven provinces from 1588 until the Batavian Revolution of 1795. The imported map covers only about 1600 to 1783. Its merchants, printers, painters and scholars flourished, while overseas companies used violence and slavery in Asia, Africa and the Americas. Families worked, learned, played and coped with household chores and illness very differently by wealth and place. The old republic ended politically in 1795; Dutch people and communities continued through the Batavian Republic and later states.

identityEvidence.assessment: Imported label and interval confirmed; historic border accuracy unverified.
